concept.body: Law of Sines: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C, where each side pairs with the angle OPPOSITE it. To use: (1) find a complete matched pair (side + its opposite angle); (2) if an angle is missing, subtract from 180°; (3) set the target's ratio equal to the pair's and solve. Keep sides glued to their own angles.

widget.prompt: A triangle has a side of 10 opposite a 90° angle. What side sits opposite the 30° angle? (sin 30° = 0.5, sin 90° = 1)

commonErrors.feedback: 20 = 10 ÷ 0.5 flips the proportion — the smaller angle takes the SMALLER side: 10 × 0.5 = 5.
10 copies the given side — but a 30° angle can't face as much side as the 90°. Scale by sin 30°: 5.

steps.body: Drop the right angle and SOH-CAH-TOA loses its footing — no hypotenuse, no “opposite the right angle.” But a quieter pattern survives in EVERY triangle: each side, divided by the sine of its opposite angle, gives the same number. **a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C** — the Law of Sines.

widget.prompt: The Law of Sines makes precise an old intuition. Which one?

options.label: Larger angles sit opposite larger sides, in exact sine proportion
options.feedback: Since side = (common ratio) × sin(opposite angle), sides scale with the sines of their angles.

options.label: All three sides of a triangle are equal
options.feedback: Only equilateral triangles manage that. The law says sides are PROPORTIONAL to opposite sines — equal only when angles are.

options.label: The largest side equals the two smaller sides combined
options.feedback: That would flatten the triangle to a segment — the triangle inequality forbids it. The law ties each side to its opposite SINE.

options.label: Angles are proportional to the sides adjacent to them
options.feedback: The pairing runs OPPOSITE, not adjacent: each angle faces the side its sine governs.

steps.body: Using it takes one matched **pair** — a side together with its opposite angle — plus one more piece. Know A = 40° with a = 12, and B = 65°: then b/sin 65° = 12/sin 40°, so b = 12·sin 65°/sin 40° ≈ 16.92. Keep each side glued to ITS angle; crossing the pairs flips the answer.

explanationVariants: b = 12·sin 65°/sin 40° ≈ 12 × 0.9063/0.6428 ≈ 16.92 — bigger than 12, as the bigger angle demands.
Set b/sin B = a/sin A and solve: b = a·sin B/sin A ≈ 16.92.

widget.prompt: In triangle ABC: A = 40°, B = 65°, and side a = 12 (opposite A). Find side b (2 decimals).

commonErrors.feedback: 8.51 = 12·sin 40°/sin 65° crosses the pairs — and shrinks the side facing the BIGGER angle, backwards. b = 12·sin 65°/sin 40° ≈ 16.92.
10.88 = 12·sin 65° multiplies but never divides by sin 40° — half the proportion. Finish it: ≈ 16.92.
18.67 = 12/sin 40° is the common RATIO itself, before multiplying by sin 65°: × 0.9063 → ≈ 16.92.

steps.body: The third angle always rides free: angles sum to 180°, so C = 180 − 40 − 65 = 75° — and the same anchor pair prices side c too. One matched pair unlocks the whole triangle. Sanity check at the end: the biggest side must face the biggest angle.

widget.prompt: The triangle has A = 40° and B = 65°. Drag corner C until angle A reads the size of the remaining angle C.
widget.successFeedback: C = 75°, since 40 + 65 + 75 = 180. This matters before any Law of Sines work: the rule pairs each angle with the side opposite it, so the third angle has to be found first or the largest side has no angle to pair with.
widget.targetFeedback: Not there yet. A and B are 40° and 65°, and the three angles total 180°.
widget.invariantFeedback: Keep an eye on the total while dragging — it stays at 180°, which is what lets you find any angle from the other two.

explanationVariants: c = 12·sin 75°/sin 40° ≈ 18.03 — the largest side, facing the largest angle (75°). ✓
Same anchor ratio 12/sin 40°, now scaled by sin 75°: ≈ 18.03.

widget.prompt: Still A = 40°, a = 12, and now C = 75°. Find side c (2 decimals).

commonErrors.feedback: 7.99 = 12·sin 40°/sin 75° crosses the pairs again — the 75° sine belongs on TOP with side c: ≈ 18.03.
11.59 = 12·sin 75° skips the division by sin 40° — the anchor pair funds the ratio: 12·sin 75°/sin 40° ≈ 18.03.

explanationVariants: The law is a proportion of side-angle PAIRS — without one complete pair, the common ratio has no value.
Three angles fix only the shape; a matched side-angle pair sets the scale.

widget.prompt: Which information is NOT enough for the Law of Sines to find a missing side?

options.label: All three angles, but no sides
options.feedback: Angles alone give shape without size — every similar copy qualifies. The law needs one matched side-angle pair as an anchor.

options.label: Two angles and any one side
options.feedback: That's plenty: the third angle is free (180° sum), making the known side half of a matched pair.

options.label: A side, its opposite angle, and another angle
options.feedback: A complete pair plus one more angle is the textbook setup — fully solvable.

options.label: A side, its opposite angle, and another side
options.feedback: A pair plus a side also works (it finds the second side's angle) — the anchor pair is there.

hints: The 60 m bank is side c, opposite the third angle C = 180 − 72 − 58 = 50° — there's your matched pair.
The distance from station A to the tree is side a... opposite angle A? Careful: it's opposite the 58° at station B.
explanationVariants: C = 50° anchors the pair: d = 60·sin 58°/sin 50° ≈ 66.42 m.
The side from A faces B's 58°: scale the ratio 60/sin 50° by sin 58° ≈ 66.42 m.

widget.prompt: Surveyors at A and B stand 60 m apart on a riverbank. A tree T sits across the river; angle A (∠TAB) = 72° and angle B (∠TBA) = 58°. Find the distance from A to the tree (2 decimals).

commonErrors.feedback: 74.49 = 60·sin 72°/sin 50° uses A's own angle on top — that computes the distance from station B (side BT faces ∠A). Side AT faces ∠B = 58°: ≈ 66.42.
54.2 = 60·sin 50°/sin 58° flips the proportion, putting the anchor's sine on top. The unknown side's sine goes on top: 60·sin 58°/sin 50° ≈ 66.42.

takeaways: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C in EVERY triangle — sides scale with opposite sines.
One matched side-angle pair anchors the ratio; the 180° sum supplies missing angles.
Audit: biggest side faces biggest angle.
steps.teaser: Next: when you have two sides hugging an angle — or all three sides — the Law of Cosines.
